title: E36 - Too Much FOMO: Why I'm Back on the Legal AI Startup Investor Train with Sandstone CEO Nick Fleisher
author: Nick Fleisher

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source shifts the explanation toward vendor-side product development: faster iteration, simpler configuration and stronger startup teams. It offers useful implementation observations but does not substantively engage the cluster’s central account of legal AI as organisational service redesign shaped by leadership, incentives, professional identity and frontline resources.
qs: So in that sense, I think because you can iterate faster, you can build more customer-centric products.
But I think with Legal, the broader problem has just been the tools that are out there have gotten so over-the-top, customized and become so hard to configure and use.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source discusses AI-enabled legal-tech product development, legacy software design and investment in founding teams. It does not address associate apprenticeship, the expertise-verification paradox, junior staffing, or deliberate training responses, so its position on the cluster proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: Contract intelligence: Business coordination exceeds document storage
st.an: Fleisher accepts the core proposition that in-house AI must organise business context and workflows beyond document analysis, and materially develops it through a concrete integrated-platform model spanning intake channels, business systems, accumulated decision data and existing CLMs. He also adds a conditional account of CLM disruption and specialist vendors’ defence against general-purpose AI, while relying mainly on product claims and anecdotes.
qs: Like, what they say to us is, we are overloaded with work, and it comes in from everywhere, and I need a single place to manage all of that work, and all of the context and data points behind everything that comes in, right?
CLMs didn't build thinking about the end-business users and how they would have to engage with the tool.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: Sandstone accepts that in-house AI can strengthen corporate legal departments and selectively reduce routine outside-counsel spending. It materially extends the proposition by specifying an in-house-focused model built around demand management, integrated business context and institutional knowledge, while presenting Harvey and CLM systems as complementary rather than necessarily displaced.
qs: And so can we also pull back some of that, which I think then let's you focus on hiring the best people internally, and making sure that the lawyers within your company are actually spending time thinking about the bigger business and strategic decisions that are related to legal.

Like, what they say to us is, we are overloaded with work, and it comes in from everywhere, and I need a single place to manage all of that work, and all of the context and data points behind everything that comes in, right?

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Fleisher accepts the value of specialist legal workflow software and materially develops the proposition by arguing that defensibility comes from niche legal knowledge, user experience and highly targeted applications that generic platforms cannot readily reproduce. He also adds a buyer-side adoption distinction: in-house teams may deploy aligned workflows faster than large law firms. The evidence is primarily experiential and predictive, and he does not substantively address human verification or autonomous delivery.
qs: We've seen legal specific vendors have done better and succeed and I think it's one of the verticals where the specific knowledge and the UX is so niche that it is such a stretch for generic tools to get into it.

Let's figure out like, what are areas where we can actually differentiate by building something that is like super pointed and targeted and different from like a Harv Hira, Legora or a Deep Judge that they could just adopt themselves.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Fleisher accepts the cluster’s core view that AI reorganises legal production rather than eliminating lawyers, and materially extends it with a concrete in-house model: routine work is integrated across enterprise systems, complex matters escalate to lawyers, and accumulated organisational decision data becomes legal infrastructure. His account particularly strengthens the cluster’s buyer-side reallocation and institutional-absorption propositions, though its performance claims are largely company-reported.
qs: And if it's something a little bit complex, you know, it'll get passed to a lawyer, they'll get a notification, they'll get asked to approve it, and it'll go back to HR.

And we've built almost a brain behind the legal team, which is like, you know, hundreds or thousands of data points on all the decisions that they've made, all the entities and companies and people they've engaged with.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that value comes from selective automation embedded in redesigned, human-led workflows, then materially extends it for in-house legal departments. It specifies that effective deployment must integrate business-system context, standardize intake and review processes, escalate complex work to lawyers, and measure ROI through responsiveness and cross-functional business outcomes rather than time savings alone.
qs: So we have to sit on top of 40, 50 systems within your existing company, whether it's Teams, Outlook, Gmail, Slack, but also then think about Salesforce, Workday, all these other business systems, which are like super important pieces of data for lawyers as they think about answering questions and reviewing documents.
And if it's something a little bit complex, you know, it'll get passed to a lawyer, they'll get a notification, they'll get asked to approve it, and it'll go back to HR.

st.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding
st.an: Fleisher supports the cluster’s conditional optimism by presenting legal AI startups as multidisciplinary career opportunities for engineers, lawyers and legal-tech professionals. However, his recruitment-focused claims are promotional and provide no evidence of product performance, adoption or broader labour-market outcomes.
qs: We are obviously hiring, I think, we've built an amazing team of engineers, lawyers and folks across legal tech.
And so, if that's you, or you're a lawyer who's interested in tech and wants to go do something more interesting, definitely reach out and we'd love to chat.

st.t: Contract infrastructure: AI challenges siloed CLM systems
st.an: Fleisher supports the synthesis’s central framing: contract management remains necessary, while incumbent CLM products face pressure from poor usability, narrow workflows and weak use of stored data. Sandstone’s strategy also exemplifies the unresolved architectural choice by supporting both integration with existing CLMs and, for some customers, full replacement.
qs: SPEAKER_2 (00:22:53) I don't think the core concepts of what CLM is and what it set out to do are dead.
And so for us, the reason we chose to integrate with everything is because I want to be able to just sit on top of that.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s emphasis on workflow-centred redesign, in-house demand and institutional implementation constraints. Fleisher argues that legal software should reflect how lawyers and business users actually work, and that adoption depends on examining matters, identifying targeted high-value uses and improving data readiness. It does not materially address pricing pressure, verification or the apprenticeship problem, and its evidence is largely experiential rather than systematic.
qs: They were built around the idea of a contract or the idea of the actual work product versus how do the lawyers and the people in the business actually work and think about legal.
So we would say, hey, let's go look at all the matters that you do and all the work that you do.

st.t: Legal data: Connected records enable operational transformation
st.an: Fleisher directly supports connecting legal workload and review workflows with business context. He argues that in-house legal teams respond to business demand and that commercial facts should inform legal judgment, while offering product examples rather than measured evidence of outcomes.
qs: A legal org in a company has to function based on the demand that they're getting from the business and the demand from external forces.
They're completely business specific concepts, but they impact how you actually go do the legal work and the way that you think about it.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: Fleisher directly supports the cluster’s central proposition by locating value in data readiness, implementation and firm-specific applications grounded in actual matters, rather than in model capability alone. His account is experience-based and does not independently address verification or establish measured performance outcomes.
qs: And so, pivoted, and a lot of our work ended up being serving M Law firms and Magic Circle firms, are not just AI strategy and use cases, but also are we in a good spot from a data perspective?

On the law firm side, the most interesting piece is just like, we had a perspective that you could, the most value we could have is coming in and building very specific things that are like high value add for your firm and the works that you do.

st.t: Vendor value: Concentration forecasts face diverse competition
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that in-house legal departments are a distinct market where value may come from improving business-facing workflows, not merely contract review. Its Sandstone leadership claim is explicitly an investor prediction and supplies no performance, retention or market-share evidence, consistent with the cluster’s caution that investment enthusiasm does not establish durable returns.
qs: It completely rewrites how legal teams interact with the business, and what my finding has been is that that is the single biggest pain point for in-house attorneys.
He's the CEO of Sandstone, a product that I believe is going to be the category leader in AI for in-house legal teams.

kp.k: Investor interview frames a second legal-AI entrepreneurial wave
kp.d: Host Zach Abramowitz discloses investing in Sandstone, his first private-company investment in three years, and presents it as part of an anticipated second wave after Harvey and Legora. His prediction of Sandstone's category leadership is an investor's judgment, not an independently demonstrated market finding. Although the document is labelled 2026, he locates his renewed investment commitments at the end of 2025.
qs: This is going to be the first private company I've invested in in three years.
I've always been confident that there was going to be a second wave of AI entrepreneurs that were going to come into this space, and that was going to be my opportunity.
But here at the end of 2025, I've committed to multiple companies.

kp.k: AI accelerates customer-led legal software development
kp.d: Fleisher attributes more customer-centric design partly to AI-enabled iteration rather than an inherently different design philosophy. He reports starting with a non-AI Kanban board and 30 users before leaving McKinsey, now shipping 40–50 PRs daily tied to customer requests. His example of producing a mock-up during a GC demonstration illustrates a claimed shift from month-long to same-day feature delivery.
qs: Initially, the first thing I built was a Kanban board for lawyers to track their work. Super simple, not even AI.
We're shipping 40, 50 PRs a day
So I can ship that feature by the end of the day instead of by the end of the month.
So in that sense, I think because you can iterate faster, you can build more customer-centric products.

kp.k: Consulting demand shifted toward AI strategy, data and implementation
kp.d: Fleisher describes McKinsey's legal-services work moving from firm strategy and private-equity diligence of legal technology into AI strategy, data readiness and bespoke development after generative AI emerged. He distinguishes targeted, differentiating firm tools from general products firms could adopt themselves, and reports work involving law firms, ALSPs and the AAA AI Arbitrator. His financial illustrations of potential bespoke-tool value are possibilities, not measured returns.
qs: private equity started coming in and buying up the legal practice management tools, the ELMs, e-discovery
Harvey, Legora come out, all these other tools, and now every law firm is coming to us saying, what do we do about AI?
It's public knowledge that we worked on the AAA's AI Arbitrator.
it might, you know, be an incremental couple hundred million somewhere.

kp.k: Firmwide adoption differs sharply from in-house deployment
kp.d: Drawing on his consulting and startup experience, Fleisher distinguishes securing initial BigLaw sponsorship from achieving widespread lawyer use. He speculates that some tools could take 20 years to move from 1% to 95% firm adoption, contrasting this with reported instances of signing an entire in-house team into Sandstone in one day. These are experience-based claims, not comparative adoption-study findings.
qs: Getting the 1% to 95% adoption within the firm is monumental.
And it could take 20 years, I think, for some of these AI tools.
And you can get an entire legal team signed into the product in one day. That does not happen in big law.

kp.k: In-house AI requires business context, not just legal documents
kp.d: Fleisher argues that in-house work involves business strategy and risk trade-offs distinct from the document-focused work he associates with law-firm tools. He describes integrating communications, CRM and HR data to inform review, drafting and answers, alongside entity repositories and demand insights. He acknowledges that senior law-firm lawyers also provide context-sensitive, bespoke advice; the contrast is his product-positioning argument rather than a universal division of legal work.
qs: In-house is truly much more of a business and strategy type role than it is a classic practice of law.
As a lawyer in a company, you end up becoming someone who has to weigh business concepts and potential risk outcomes with the legal work that you're doing.
For a lawyer within a law firm, you might do some of that, especially when you're more senior and you're giving bespoke guidance to clients.
A legal org in a company has to function based on the demand that they're getting from the business and the demand from external forces.

kp.k: Workflow orchestration can complement specialist AI and CLM
kp.d: Fleisher reports multiple customers using Harvey alongside Sandstone: customers seek centralized requests and business context from Sandstone while using Harvey for deeper document interrogation. He similarly reports integration with almost all CLMs, with almost every client having one, though some are migrating away. This presents coexistence and selective replacement rather than inevitable wholesale substitution.
qs: We have multiple customers using Harvey.
I need a single knowledge layer that centralizes all the requests and things that we get from the business.
We integrate with almost all of them, and every one of our clients has a CLM, almost.
Now, some of them are migrating off of their CLM and using us fully at this point.

kp.k: CLM faces conditional displacement, despite substantial switching barriers
kp.d: Fleisher says CLM's underlying objectives remain relevant but argues incumbent tools struggle with AI capabilities, usability and workflows extending beyond contracts. He identifies difficult implementation and removal as their principal moat, motivating Sandstone's overlay strategy. His prediction that the category could die is conditional on failure to make stored data usable in analysis and contract review, not a claim that CLM has already disappeared.
qs: I don't think the core concepts of what CLM is and what it set out to do are dead.
the biggest moat that the CLMs have is that they're incredibly hard to set up, and they're incredibly hard to rip out.

But if CLMs, I think, don't adapt to be able to understand the data that sits inside of them, actually embed that data, allow people to ask questions, to sort it, to use it as part of their contract review processes, I think the CLM as a category could die.
What lawyers do in companies goes way beyond contracts

kp.k: Embedded intake avoids imposing new tools on business users
kp.d: Fleisher criticizes CLM for neglecting end-business users and overemphasizing sales and procurement. His proposed alternative captures requests through existing communication channels and consolidates them for lawyers. He links rigid, company-specific workflows to lengthy implementations, while explicitly resisting blaming legal operations professionals for difficulties with vendors and tools.
qs: CLMs didn't build thinking about the end-business users and how they would have to engage with the tool.
Let's just meet them in Slack. Let's meet them in Gmail. Let's meet them wherever they are, right? And bring all of that to the lawyers in one single platform, right?
I don't want to like bash legal ops, folks. It's a tough job.

kp.k: ROI includes business relationships and operational enablement
kp.d: Fleisher rejects time-to-resolution as sufficient because legal matters involve iterative exchanges and negotiation. He proposes business satisfaction, visibility into legal work and faster business execution as additional measures. An HR example describes a bot consulting Workday and past agreements, with more complex requests routed to lawyer approval; the suggested 15-minute completion is illustrative, not a reported study result or assurance of autonomous legal reliability.
qs: the biggest one ultimately is like, do folks in the business feel like they are working more closely and, you know, not seeing legal as much of a black box as they might today?
is legal actively helping us drive business
if it's something a little bit complex, you know, it'll get passed to a lawyer, they'll get a notification, they'll get asked to approve it, and it'll go back to HR.
That could happen in like 15 minutes, right?

kp.k: Automation could redirect lawyers toward strategy and risk
kp.d: Fleisher relays lawyers' complaints of spending 70% of their day on administrative tasks and proposes reducing this to 30 or 40% as a meaningful outcome, not an achieved result. He also advocates reducing outside-counsel spending on basic work and using the resulting capacity to support stronger internal hiring, business decisions and serious risk discussions. The emphasis is task reallocation and insourcing rather than documented job losses.
qs: I feel like I spend 70% of my day doing admin type things that are crazy given my background and the work that I'm actually paid to do.
if I can take that 70% and make that like 30 or 40%, that's a huge win for us and for everyone
making sure that the lawyers within your company are actually spending time thinking about the bigger business and strategic decisions that are related to legal.
And you can actually focus on risk more too.

kp.k: AI mandates and shared benefits expand potential purchasing budgets
kp.d: Fleisher says sales usually target lawyers, sometimes legal operations or CIOs, and involve business units as use cases develop. He attributes greater spending capacity to executive AI mandates, potential risk improvements and benefits to sales and other functions, reporting GCs considering CRO funding. Abramowitz separately reports a Wharton study showing a 24-percentage-point adoption increase over the last year; the transcript supplies no study methodology or sample details.
qs: for the most part, we're selling to lawyers
I've seen a lot of CEOs who will just put out a KPI, which is like, is legal using some AI system.
I've had GC say, well, I'm going to go ask our CRO for some budget for this because it's going to change the way that they do business.
the Wharton study just came out, showed that the legal function within businesses has seen the sharpest increase in adoption over the last year, full 24 percentage points

kp.k: Standardized AI workflows could broaden legal risk coverage
kp.d: Fleisher contrasts permissive adoption of individual point solutions with structured departmental use of common playbooks and data. He argues that greater processing capacity could bring previously bypassed or late-arriving work into one review system, improving visibility and risk management. This is explicitly a theoretical benefit, not evidence that AI has reduced legal errors or losses.
qs: let lawyers use whatever tool they want, any point solution versus, like, let's build something that is structured and everyone is leveraging the same playbooks and concepts and data sources.
take this long tail of work, which happens in some companies where legal is involved super last minute, or they're not involved at all, and start to funnel it through one system
in theory, your risk tolerance is going to be better and you're going to be able to manage and mitigate risk much more closely because you see everything.

kp.k: Consolidation may redirect spending from incumbent software
kp.d: Fleisher argues many in-house departments have bought little legal-specific technology, citing an 85-person team using Google Drive and Gmail as a rare anecdote. He considers current legal-tech spending below its appropriate level while estimating CLMs are 30–50% overpriced and signature tools 80–90% overpriced. These are his commercial judgments, supporting a proposed reallocation of incumbent-tool budgets rather than measured market-wide pricing findings.
qs: I talked to an 85-person legal team yesterday that uses Google Drive and Gmail.
Now, that's rare and that's an anomaly.
I think CLMs are 30 to 50% overpriced. I think signature tools are 80 to 90% overpriced
can I start to consolidate these and maybe cut some of these old costs that I've had and shift them towards other places?

kp.k: Specialization and integrations underpin the claimed vertical-software moat
kp.d: Fleisher disputes the reported view that OpenAI is Harvey's largest competitor, arguing legal-specific knowledge, interfaces and data integration make generic entry difficult. He allows frontier labs could win in areas such as coding, but regards legal as relatively niche and specialized. He describes Sandstone's 45 system connections and accumulated decision data as departmental infrastructure; this is a founder's defensibility thesis, not a demonstrated barrier against future competition.
qs: Harvey came out and said, OpenAI is our biggest competitor. I just don't think that's true.
the specific knowledge and the UX is so niche that it is such a stretch for generic tools to get into it.
legal is one where like it's a big market, but it's not like, you know, DevTools size and it's very specific.
our tool connects to 45 other systems.
That inherently is infrastructure for the legal team.

kp.k: Lawyers increasingly participate in software building
kp.d: Fleisher reports interviewing 250 lawyers since founding Sandstone and having five lawyers coding daily, interpreting this as increased enthusiasm for technology careers. Some are trained software engineers; others update prompts and make small changes under engineering oversight. He sees accessible coding as beneficial to iteration but distinguishes quickly building a tool from maintaining a scalable product across many companies.
qs: since starting this company, I've interviewed 250 lawyers.
we have five lawyers on our team who are coding every day.
even the ones who aren't are able to go in and update prompts and make small changes as long as engineers are overseeing it.
The difference between vibe coding something quickly and actually building a scaled product which can customize and work for many different companies is massive.

kp.k: Simpler integration challenges implementation-intensive delivery models
kp.d: Fleisher claims some clients integrate 8–10 systems in a week, with user-facing field mapping potentially completed independently in an hour. He says Sandstone currently implements effectively itself despite discussions with implementation partners. Abramowitz argues consultant-free adoption reduces conflicting incentives, while Fleisher predicts immediate, visible value will become a software purchasing expectation. The deployment timings remain vendor-reported capabilities.
qs: We have some clients where we are literally integrated into, you know, 8 to 10 systems. And, by the way, we can do that in a week.
it can happen in an hour on their own instead of us having to send in six implementation specialists to get it done.
If you're able to have a product that gets adoption without implementation specialists, it limits the number of parties whose incentives you have to care about
I should be able to open something and start using it and see some value.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Nick Fleisher predicts that AI-native, business-integrated software will change in-house legal workflows, while arguing that specialised legal software remains defensible against generic AI tools.
pts.d: Fleisher makes several connected claims. First, AI accelerates software development and customer feedback, enabling more customer-centric legal products. Second, in-house teams can adopt tools and obtain value much faster than large law firms, where broad adoption can be difficult despite initial purchasing enthusiasm. Third, in-house AI needs business context and integrated request management rather than only research or document analysis: he positions Sandstone as a central knowledge and workflow layer that can complement Harvey and existing contract lifecycle management (CLM) systems. Fourth, AI can shift legal from a back-office function toward enabling business activity, automate routine agreement workflows, reduce administrative work and basic outside-counsel expenditure, and free lawyers for strategy and risk discussions. Fifth, centralising more reviews and applying consistent playbooks could improve risk visibility and mitigation. Sixth, legacy CLM concepts remain useful, but vendors or the category could be displaced if they fail to make their data usable with AI; difficult replacement protects incumbents, so integration can precede substitution. Seventh, AI mandates, cross-functional business benefits and consolidation of existing software expenditure can expand funding for in-house technology. Eighth, niche workflows, data integrations and scalable deployment distinguish legal software businesses from quickly replicated features or generic AI products. Finally, AI-assisted development enables lawyers to contribute directly to building software, under engineering oversight. These are Fleisher's claims as Sandstone's CEO, not independent findings or the host's investment predictions.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is primarily Fleisher's consulting experience, customer conversations, product-development experience and self-reported deployment examples; projected benefits are not presented as measured outcomes.
pts.d: Fleisher draws on legal-technology diligence and AI implementation work at McKinsey, including work for large law firms and on the American Arbitration Association's AI Arbitrator. For Sandstone, he reports 30 initial users, rapid customer-request-led development, customers simultaneously using Harvey, integration with existing CLMs, some customers moving off CLM, and clients integrated with eight to ten systems within a week. He describes an HR workflow drawing on Workday and previous agreements, with lawyer approval for somewhat complex requests, that could complete in about 15 minutes. This is a capability illustration rather than a documented time-saving study. Lawyers' reports of spending 70% of their day on administration support his proposed reduction to 30–40%, but he supplies no measured before-and-after result. Budget claims rely on conversations with executives and GCs, CEO adoption mandates, and examples of proposed cross-functional funding. His estimates that CLMs and signature products are overpriced are opinions without a disclosed pricing analysis. His claim that legal AI attracts lawyers into technology is supported by his report of interviewing 250 lawyers and employing five lawyers who code. The episode provides no independent benchmark, systematic adoption dataset, measured legal accuracy result or quantified causal ROI study for these claims. The host discloses investing in Sandstone; the host's separately cited Wharton statistic and third-party opinions are not treated as Fleisher's evidence.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Fleisher combines current product and customer reports with conditional forecasts; most market-wide changes have no fixed deadline.
pts.d: The document is labelled 2026, while the host situates the conversation at the end of 2025. Fleisher presents rapid iteration, customer coexistence with Harvey and CLMs, and integrations as current capabilities or experiences. His operational examples range from a same-day feature release and one-day team sign-in to week-long integrations and an approximately 15-minute HR workflow. Sign-in should not be equated with sustained adoption. His suggestion that some law-firm tools could take 20 years to progress from 1% to 95% adoption is explicitly speculative, not a forecast for every firm or product. Reduced administration and outside-counsel spending are opportunities or targets, not established realised savings. Improved risk management is explicitly qualified as theoretical and depends on centralising more work in a consistent system. CLM disappearance depends on failure to adapt; existing implementations and useful document stores support coexistence in the meantime. Generic AI encroachment is not ruled out universally: Fleisher acknowledges that major labs could win in areas such as coding, but considers legal too specialised for imminent takeover. Lawyer participation in software changes is qualified by engineer supervision. His expectation of immediate product value is a forward-looking market norm, without a dated adoption schedule.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are corporate legal teams and their business colleagues, with implications for outside counsel, incumbent vendors, implementation consultants and lawyers entering technology careers.
pts.d: For in-house counsel and GCs, Fleisher envisages unified intake, access to business context, less administrative work, more consistent review and more capacity for strategic and risk work. The described workflow combines automation with human approval for more complex requests rather than asserting unrestricted autonomous legal decision-making. For sales, HR and procurement, the proposed benefit is faster, more visible interaction with legal through tools they already use, such as Slack or Gmail. These functions may also contribute budget where legal technology helps their work. Legal operations and IT are buyers or implementation participants; existing CLM data can be retained and mapped rather than discarded. Outside law firms could lose basic work brought in-house, while large law firms themselves face slower internal AI adoption and may benefit from narrowly targeted bespoke tools. CLM and signature vendors face consolidation and pricing pressure, and CLM implementation partners may need new opportunities as simpler deployment reduces specialist requirements. Specialised legal-AI vendors are portrayed as differentiated by domain knowledge, integrations and user experience. Lawyers interested in technology gain opportunities to join product teams and contribute to coding or prompt updates. The source concerns enterprise legal operations and legal software markets, not access to justice or demonstrated profession-wide employment displacement.
